# Self-hosted STT for ClassPulse: local benchmark vs Sarvam Saaras v3

*Run 2026-10-12 on one Windows laptop (RTX 5050 Laptop 8 GB). Everything here can be re-run from `X:\Projects\stt-bench` (see `README.md`). This file is generated by `scripts/make_report.py` from `scripts/report_text.py` and `results/tables.md`.*

## Summary

**No open model tested here can replace Saaras v3 codemix today as a drop-in for Tamil–English classroom audio.**
The gap is in code-mixed, noisy, long classroom speech, not in clean Indic read speech:

1. **AI4Bharat IndicConformer 600M multilingual (MIT)** is the best self-hosted model for *native-language* speech. On FLEURS it scores
   macro WER **16.5% (RNNT) / 16.4% (CTC)** across 9 Indic languages, against **13.9%** for Saaras. Its CER is 5.1% against 4.4%, and
   the confidence intervals overlap in most languages. It is very fast: RTF 0.03–0.06 on the laptop GPU, and **0.055–0.09 on 8 CPU
   threads** (it does not need a GPU). It has two blocking problems on our lectures:
   - it writes every English word in Indic script ("programming language" → "ப்ரோக்ராமிங் லாங்குவேஜ்"), so English-term retention is **0%**;
   - on real classroom audio it drops most of the speech: 137 of Saaras's 1,121 words on 60 s windows, and 320 words with 20 s chunking.
     It holds up on one of three recordings and collapses on the noisier two.
2. **Whisper large-v3 (faster-whisper, auto language detection)** comes closest to Saaras on the code-mixed lectures. Its agreement CER is
   42% overall and about 20% on the English-heavy Java lecture, and it keeps 63% of English terms in Latin script. But it is poor on
   native-script Indic (FLEURS macro WER 70%). It hallucinates when the language is forced on noisy audio, and it is slow on this GPU
   (RTF 0.43 at beam 5). Turbo is 5× faster but sometimes *translates* Tamil speech into English.
3. **OpenAI whisper-1, the current production fallback, is unusable for 5 of the 9 languages.** The API rejects `bn, gu, ml, pa, te` as
   language codes. With auto-detect it then writes the wrong script (Bengali comes back in Gujarati script, Punjabi in Devanagari),
   giving WER 85–104%.

4. **LLM post-correction does not close the gap.** A follow-up phase ran IndicConformer (and Whisper) output through
   `gpt-4.1-mini` and a local Qwen3-8B (4-bit, llama.cpp) with a guarded, segment-preserving prompt:
   - On FLEURS, gpt-4.1-mini improves IndicConformer macro WER from 16.5% to **15.9%** (Saaras 13.9%), mostly in Malayalam.
     Qwen3-8B changes almost nothing.
   - On classroom audio, the LLM can only fix words the recogniser produced. IndicConformer drops most of the speech, so agreement only
     moves from 91 to 85 WER, and English-term retention from 0 to 14%.
   - Whisper + GPT goes from 55.0 to 52.9 agreement WER, and retention from 63% to 67%.
   - Cost is small: ≈ ₹2–5 per lecture-hour for gpt-4.1-mini; for Qwen3-8B, 5–11 GPU-minutes per lecture-hour on the 8 GB laptop GPU.
     See "LLM post-correction" below.

**Recommendation.**
- **Keep Saaras v3 in production for now.**
- **Start a self-hosting track built on IndicConformer 600M** (MIT, CPU-capable, 2.4 GB). It could run on a GPU box or even on CPU next to
  the API. To become a replacement it needs three things:
  - (a) VAD segmentation into ≤ 20 s pieces;
  - (b) a **fine-tune on ~20–50 h of human-labelled ClassPulse classroom audio** with English terms written in Latin script (its
    per-language tokenizers have no Latin symbols, so this means extending the vocabulary or adding a Latin-script head);
  - (c) re-running this benchmark on a held-out classroom set.
- In parallel, **fine-tune Whisper-large-v3-turbo on the same data.** Whisper already emits Latin English inside Tamil text, so it is the
  lower-risk route to good code-mix behaviour.
- The real deliverable is **human-labelled classroom data**. Without it nobody, including us, can measure accuracy against Saaras on what
  matters.

Within the cost caps we used **61.4 min of Saaras (≈ ₹31), 61.4 min of whisper-1 (≈ $0.37) and ~35k/18k prompt/completion
tokens of gpt-4.1-mini (≈ $0.043 ≈ ₹4)**.

## Setup

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5050 Laptop, 8 GB, Blackwell sm_120, driver 591.97 (WDDM; shared with the desktop and Chrome) |
| CPU / RAM | AMD Ryzen 9 8940HX 16C/32T; 15 GB RAM, about 2–6 GB free while running |
| OS / Python | Windows 11 Home; Python 3.12.10 |
| Main env (`venv`) | torch 2.11.0+cu128 (`cuda.is_available()` True, fp16 matmul OK on sm_120), transformers 5.19.0, faster-whisper 1.2.1 / **CTranslate2 4.8.2 (runs on sm_120 with CUDA fp16; no transformers fallback needed)**, jiwer 4.0.0, indic-nlp-library 0.92 |
| NeMo env (`venv-nemo`) | AI4Bharat NeMo fork `nemo-v2` (commit 8dce88c, reports 1.23.0rc0). Installed `--no-deps` because it requires `triton`, which has no Windows wheel. Uses transformers 4.41.2, huggingface_hub 0.23.2, numpy 2.2.6 plus a 4-line `np.sctypes` shim in our script (no library code changed) |
| Decoding | Whisper-family: beam 5, `condition_on_previous_text=False`, no VAD. Qwen3-ASR / Canary / Parakeet: greedy (HF defaults). CTC: greedy. IndicConformer: greedy, fp16 autocast. Batch size 1 for everything |
| Timing | RTF = processing wall time ÷ audio duration, after one warm-up call, excluding model load. Peak VRAM = `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated` (CTranslate2 is invisible to torch, so nvidia-smi sampling every 0.5 s is also shown; it includes other apps). Peak RAM = sampled process RSS |

**Normalisation for WER/CER:** Unicode NFC → indic-nlp-library `IndicNormalizerFactory` per language (Indic only) → every character
that is not a letter, combining mark or digit becomes a space (this removes punctuation, danda and hyphens) → Latin lower-cased →
whitespace collapsed. Digits are left as they are (no number verbalisation). For English we also report WER after OpenAI's Whisper
`EnglishTextNormalizer` (contractions, number formatting, spelling). WER and CER are corpus-level (total edits ÷ total reference
words/chars). The 95% CIs are percentile bootstrap over utterances (1,000 resamples; n = 25 per cell).

**Code-mixed lecture metrics:** there is no human transcript, so Saaras v3 codemix output is the **reference for agreement only**.
- **Agreement WER/CER** compares each model against Saaras.
- **English-term retention** = share of Saaras's Latin-script tokens of ≥ 3 letters that also appear in Latin script in the candidate
  (multiset match).
- **Script-agnostic phonetic CER** (extra) romanises Tamil script (ISO), strips vowels and diacritics, and merges voiced/unvoiced and
  aspirated pairs. It asks "did the model hear the same sounds?" whatever the script, so "மீடியன்" and "median" score as close.

## Datasets

| Set | Exact source | Licence | Sample |
|---|---|---|---|
| FLEURS test | `google/fleurs`, revision `refs/convert/parquet`, `<lang>/test/0000.parquet` for hi_in, ta_in, te_in, kn_in, ml_in, bn_in, mr_in, gu_in, pa_in, en_us | CC-BY-4.0 | 25 utterances per language, seed `20261012`, one per sentence id, 2–20 s. **9 Indic + English = 250 utterances, 48.1 min.** Ids are in `data/manifest.jsonl` (`source` field gives the parquet row) |
| Indian-accented English | **NPTEL2020** (AI4Bharat, Indian-English lecture speech) as redistributed in `skbose/indian-english-nptel-test` (ungated; the repo states no licence; NPTEL content is CC BY-SA). Three seeded remote row groups from files 00000, 00026 and 00050 | CC BY-SA (upstream) | 25 utterances, 24 speakers, 3.3 min. The references are cleaned subtitles, **not verbatim**: disfluencies are dropped, "that's" is written "that is", and so on. Every system scores 20–28% WER, and much of that is reference noise |
| Svarah (`ai4bharat/Svarah`) | — | CC-BY-4.0 | **Skipped: gated** (`gated=auto`, needs an HF login and accepting terms). NPTEL was used instead |
| Kathbath / Lahaja / IndicVoices (`ai4bharat/*`) | — | — | **Skipped: all gated** (`gated=auto`). Third-party re-uploads exist on HF, but we did not use them to get around the gates. SPRINGLab IndicVoices-R mirrors are open, but they are 4.4 GB shards of the *train* split (contamination risk), so we skipped them too |
| Real classroom audio | 4 local recordings copied (not moved) from the ClassPulse repo into `stt-bench/audio/` | private | 10 × 60 s windows (10.0 min): lec1 at 10 s and 80 s; lec2 at 150, 600 and 1080 s; lec3 at 90 and 420 s; lec4 at 200, 720 and 1260 s. Saaras detected **lec1, lec2 and lec4 as Tamil–English code-mix** (8 windows; statistics, Java/JDBC and statistics lectures). **lec3 is Indian English** (2 windows, banking/cyber-security). Local models got the whole 60 s window; Saaras got 2 × 30 s pieces |

Reading the overall table:
- **IndicConformer is statistically tied with Saaras in most single languages** (hi, te, bn, pa, gu: overlapping CIs). It is behind on
  ta, kn, ml and mr by 2–5 WER points.
- Language-specific fine-tunes (IndicWhisper-medium, ARTPARK Vaani-Whisper large-v3) are competitive in their one language. Hindi:
  14.9–16.9 against Saaras 12.2. Telugu: 14.4–15.2 against 12.8. Tamil: IndicWhisper 20.6 against 18.5. But you would need one model per
  language.
- Massively multilingual models (MMS-1B-all, omniASR CTC 1B) land at 27–30% WER, and stock Whisper at 70–77%.
- On English (FLEURS en-US), everyone is within noise: 3.9–7.2%, with Qwen3-ASR-1.7B best at 3.9%. MMS and omniASR are the exception at
  12–19%.
- On Indian-English lecture speech (NPTEL), Whisper large-v3 is best (18–20%). Saaras, Canary, Parakeet, Qwen3 and whisper-1 sit at
  24–28%, but the reference noise above dominates and the CIs are wide.

| Recording | whisper-1 | fw large-v3 (ta forced) | fw large-v3 (auto) | fw turbo (auto) | IndicConformer RNNT 20 s chunks | IndicWhisper-ta | omniASR-CTC-1B | MMS-1B (tam) |

What the lecture numbers say:
- All local models disagree with Saaras on ≥ 42% of characters for Tamil–English speech. Saaras is not ground truth (see the
  "மீன் தான் median" excerpt below, where Saaras itself writes *mean* as the Tamil word for fish). Even so, these gaps are far too large
  to be reference noise.
- Whisper large-v3 with auto-detect agrees best overall and keeps English terms in Latin script (63%).
- IndicConformer and IndicWhisper write English in Tamil script (0% retention). Their *phonetic* CER shows something different:
  IndicWhisper (38.9) and MMS (38.5) are about as close to what was said as Whisper (34–37). They are spelling English in the wrong
  script, not mishearing it. IndicConformer (72) actually loses content.
- On the English lecture (lec3) every decent English model agrees with Saaras within 8–17% WER. Qwen3-ASR 8.2, Whisper large-v3 9.2 and
  whisper-1 9.5 are the closest.

## Per-model notes

| Model | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Sarvam saaras:v3 (API) | ✅ | Sync `/speech-to-text`. FLEURS/NPTEL used `mode=transcribe` with the language set; lectures used `mode=codemix`, `language_code=unknown`, `with_timestamps=true`. **Each 60 s window was split into 2 × 30 s pieces** (sync limit) and the pieces concatenated. 3 requests failed with an SSL EOF and were retried successfully. Timestamps are chunk-level only (≈ one chunk per 30 s piece). Sarvam now also offers `saaras:v4` (default, `keyterms` biasing), which was not tested because production uses v3 |
| OpenAI whisper-1 (API) | ⚠️ | Returns HTTP 400 `unsupported_language` for **bn, gu, ml, pa, te**. Those were re-sent with auto-detect and returned the wrong script. Fine for English and Indian English |
| Whisper large-v3 / large-v3-turbo (faster-whisper, CT2 fp16) | ✅ | CTranslate2 4.8.2 works on sm_120 out of the box. Weights: `Systran/faster-whisper-large-v3`, `mobiuslabsgmbh/faster-whisper-large-v3-turbo` (MIT conversions of OpenAI weights). Native-script Indic is poor: ml 115% WER (repetition/hallucination). Forcing `language=ta` on noisy lec4 hallucinated mixed CJK/Hangul text; auto-detect was more robust on lectures. Turbo with auto-detect sometimes **translates** to English (lec1). Segment timestamps natively, word timestamps optional, long-form via 30 s sliding windows and VAD |
| AI4Bharat IndicConformer 600M multilingual | ✅ (via AI4Bharat's public object store) | The HF repo `ai4bharat/indic-conformer-600m-multilingual` (ONNX + `trust_remote_code`) is **gated** (`GatedRepoError` without login). The same model is published openly as a `.nemo` at `objectstore.e2enetworks.net/indicconformer/models/indicconformer_stt_multi_hybrid_rnnt_600m.nemo` (linked from github.com/AI4Bharat/IndicConformerASR, MIT), so we ran that through AI4Bharat's NeMo fork. Both decoders were tested; CTC ≈ RNNT. 22 languages, one tokenizer per language, **no English and no Latin symbols**. Breaks on 60 s inputs (drops most words), so use ≤ 20 s chunks or VAD. RNNT hypotheses expose per-token frame indices (`Hypothesis.timestep`, 40 ms frames), so segment timestamps are derivable; the fork's built-in `compute_timestamps` path crashes for the multilingual tokenizer (CTC: `ids_to_text() missing 'lang'`) |
| Meta MMS-1B-all + per-language adapters | ✅ | **Licence CC-BY-NC-4.0: non-commercial, cannot be used in ClassPulse.** Good CER (7.5% macro) but WER 30%, since it spells words slightly wrong; character soup on noisy lectures |
| Meta Omnilingual ASR CTC 300M / 1B (v2) | ✅ (community HF port) | The official `facebook/omniASR-CTC-*` checkpoints need fairseq2 (Linux only; WSL not attempted). We used `aadel4/omniASR-CTC-{300M,1B}-v2`, a `Wav2Vec2ForCTC` safetensors conversion whose card claims numerical parity (atol 1e-4) with fairseq2. No custom code. Apache-2.0 upstream. Language-agnostic CTC (no language parameter), so it emits whatever script it hears: Latin for English words in the Java lecture (39% retention), garbage on noisy Tamil. The 1B model is clearly better than 300M. The LLM-decoder variants (with language conditioning) were not tried |
| Bodhan AI Indic-Transcribe core / flex | ⛔ skipped | **Gated** (`gated=auto`, accept licence + share contact info). Card: canary-1b-v2 base, 25 languages, claims an 8.7 average "OIWER" against 10.7 for Saaras v3 on its own benchmark. Licence is the *Indic Open Model License v1.0*: commercial use allowed, but **hosting the model as an API/service for others needs Bodhan AI's written sign-off**, plus share-alike. Its card says English words inside Indic speech are rendered **in native script**, which is the opposite of what we need. Third-party ONNX re-uploads exist and were not used |
| IISc/ARTPARK SraVaani 1.0 | ⛔ skipped | **Gated** (`gated=auto`), MIT, FastConformer hybrid TDT-CTC, ~430M, 65 Indian languages; needs `trust_remote_code` and an HF token. Worth testing once someone accepts the terms |
| ARTPARK Vaani Whisper-large-v3 (hi, te) | ✅ | Open, Apache-2.0, standard Whisper weights (no custom code). Good in-language (hi 14.9, te 15.2) but slow (RTF 0.7–1.4 at beam 5 in transformers) and one model per language. Other Vaani FastConformer repos are gated |
| Vistaar / IndicWhisper (AI4Bharat) | ✅ (official object store) | `indicwhisper.objectstore.e2enetworks.net/{tamil,telugu,hindi}_models.zip`, MIT; Whisper-medium fine-tunes, one per language. We extracted only config/tokenizer/`pytorch_model.bin` (no `zero_to_fp32.py` or training pickles). Trained **without timestamp tokens**, so long audio was chunked at fixed 30 s. Strong per language (ta 20.6, te 14.4, hi 16.9), transliterates English into Tamil script |
| Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (Jan 2026, Apache-2.0) | ✅ (hi, en only) | Best English (FLEURS 3.9%, lec3 8.2% agreement); Hindi 18.9%. **No Tamil, Telugu or other Dravidian/East-Indic languages** in its 30-language list, so it does not fit ClassPulse. Timestamps need the separate Qwen3 forced aligner |
| NVIDIA Parakeet-TDT-0.6b-v3, Canary-1b-v2 (CC-BY-4.0) | ✅ (English only) | Native transformers classes (no NeMo needed). English/European languages only. Parakeet is very fast (RTF 0.016 on lectures) with word timestamps (TDT); Canary dropped content on lec3 (255 of 294 words) |
| ai4bharat/indic-seamless, per-language IndicConformer HF repos | ⛔ | Gated, and indic-seamless is CC-BY-NC anyway |
| MERaLiON-3-3B-ASR, granite-speech, Voxtral | not run | MERaLiON's custom licence plus ~6.6 GB of weights (too tight for 8 GB alongside the desktop). Granite needs `trust_remote_code` from a publisher outside the allowed list. Voxtral has no Dravidian-language claims |

`trust_remote_code=True` was **never used**. Pickle-format weights were loaded only from AI4Bharat (the IndicConformer `.nemo`
checkpoint through NeMo, and the IndicWhisper `pytorch_model.bin` through transformers' `weights_only` loader). Everything else is
safetensors or CTranslate2. All downloads live in `data/raw` and `models/`; no code was run from them.

| IndicConformer RNNT, CPU 8 threads | 0.09 | ~5.4 min | ~270 |
| faster-whisper large-v3-turbo, GPU | 0.07–0.095 | ~5 min | ~250–330 |
| faster-whisper large-v3, GPU, beam 5 | 0.43 | ~26 min | ~55 (a batched pipeline or L4/A10-class GPU should give ~4–10×) |

**Integration sketch.** Build an `stt-sidecar` (FastAPI, Docker) on a separate box. That is a GPU box for Whisper. For IndicConformer
CPU inference it could be a second ARM/x86 VM; only Whisper strictly needs a GPU.
- **Endpoints:**
  - `POST /speech-to-text`, Sarvam-compatible: multipart `file`, `model`, `mode`, `language_code`, `with_timestamps` →
    `{request_id, transcript, language_code, timestamps:{words,start_time_seconds,end_time_seconds}}`. The ClassPulse API would then
    only need a base-URL switch.
  - `POST /v1/audio/transcriptions`, OpenAI-compatible: `verbose_json` with `segments[]`.
- **Pipeline:**
  1. ffmpeg decode to 16 kHz mono;
  2. Silero VAD into ≤ 20 s segments (this also gives citation timestamps);
  3. per-segment language ID (Whisper LID or the AI4Bharat LID);
  4. route Indic segments to IndicConformer RNNT and English-dominant segments to Whisper-turbo or Parakeet;
  5. *(needed for IndicConformer)* back-transliterate English loanwords from Indic script to Latin, using a dictionary of the course's
     technical terms or an LLM post-edit, until a fine-tuned model writes Latin directly;
  6. join with segment times.
- **Rollout:** run it in **shadow mode** next to Saaras on real lectures, log both, and switch only when a human-labelled set shows parity.

## Cost comparison

- **Saaras v3:** about ₹30 per lecture-hour (this run: 61.4 min ≈ ₹31).
- **Self-hosted CPU (IndicConformer):** ~₹0 marginal on an existing VM if it has spare cores; one 8-thread x86 VM handles roughly
  270–440 lecture-hours a day at 100% load. On OCI Ampere ARM, expect slower per-core speed. **Measure before relying on it.**
- **Dedicated GPU (Whisper or IndicConformer):** cost per lecture-hour ≈ GPU price per hour × RTF ÷ utilisation. At an *assumed* ₹60–90
  per GPU-hour for an L4-class cloud GPU (check current Indian prices):
  - IndicConformer at RTF ≈ 0.03 costs ₹2–3 per lecture-hour when the GPU is busy;
  - Whisper large-v3 batched at RTF ≈ 0.05–0.1 costs ₹3–9 per lecture-hour.
- **Break-even for an always-on GPU** (₹45k–65k a month) against Saaras at ₹30 per hour is **~1,500–2,200 lecture-hours a month (~50–70
  a day)**. Below that, Saaras or per-second serverless GPUs are cheaper.
- Engineering and labelling cost (below) dominates at pilot scale.

## Risks and next steps

- **Small samples.** n = 25 per FLEURS language (CIs ±4–8 WER points) and 10 lecture minutes from 4 recordings and 3 teachers. Rankings
  between close models (IndicConformer against Saaras per language) are not settled.
- **FLEURS is read Wikipedia sentences** in quiet rooms. IndicConformer's near-parity there did not carry over to classrooms.
- **No ground truth for classrooms.** Saaras is the reference and it makes errors itself ("மீன் தான் median"). Agreement favours models
  that write like Saaras.
- **Untested here:**
  - the gated models (Bodhan Indic-Transcribe, SraVaani, the IndicConformer HF/ONNX build): someone has to accept their terms;
    Bodhan's service-hosting clause needs legal review;
  - ARM CPU speed;
  - batched or `int8` throughput;
  - 45–60 min end-to-end runs;
  - Saaras v4.
- **Next steps:**
  1. **Label 3–5 h of ClassPulse lectures** (Tamil, plus Telugu/Hindi if the pilot uses them), with English terms in Latin script and
     with timestamps. This is the test set every decision depends on. Then 20–50 h for fine-tuning.
  2. On a bigger GPU (24 GB, e.g. L4, A10 or 4090), re-run `queue.sh` with:
     - full FLEURS test sets;
     - faster-whisper `BatchedInferencePipeline` and `int8_float16`;
     - Whisper large-v3 *fine-tuned* on the labelled code-mix data;
     - IndicConformer fine-tuned with a Latin-script head;
     - the gated models after accepting their terms;
     - MERaLiON-3-3B-ASR (Singapore; claims Tamil code-switch);
     - 60-minute end-to-end runs with VAD.
  3. Measure IndicConformer on an OCI Ampere A1 instance (PyTorch aarch64 or the ONNX export) to see whether the existing server could
     transcribe without a GPU.
  4. Prototype the back-transliteration step (Indic-script English → Latin) and measure English-term retention again.

## LLM post-correction (follow-up phase)

**Question:** can "good local STT + an LLM that cleans the transcript" match Saaras for our classrooms?

**Setup**

- **Inputs:**
  - IndicConformer-600M **RNNT** on FLEURS (RNNT and CTC are tied, 16.5 vs 16.4; RNNT was picked because it also gives token
    timestamps) — 225 Indic utterances;
  - the IndicConformer RNNT **20 s-chunk** output on the 8 Tamil–English lecture windows, 3 segments per window (the best IndicConformer
    variant on lectures);
  - for comparison, **Whisper large-v3 (auto)** on the same windows, using its own segments (115 in total).
- **Correctors:**
  - **a) `gpt-4.1-mini`** through the OpenAI API (temperature 0, JSON mode);
  - **b) Qwen3-8B Q4_K_M** (official `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF`, Apache-2.0) on **llama.cpp b11559, Windows CUDA 13.4 build**. Blackwell
    sm_120 works with no fallback. All layers ran on the GPU, with 8k context, flash-attention, thinking disabled and JSON mode.
  - Qwen3-8B ran fine, so the smaller fallbacks (Qwen3-4B / Gemma-3-4B) were not needed.
- **Sarvam open LLMs were not run.** sarvam-m (24B dense) and sarvam-30b (19.6 GB at Q4_K_M) do not fit 8 GB of VRAM plus ~5 GB of free
  RAM. sarvam-1 is a 2B *base* (non-instruct) model, not suitable for instruction-following correction.

**Prompt** (`scripts/llm_correct.py`):
- Fix only obvious recognition errors. Never paraphrase, summarise, translate, reorder, add or remove; when unsure, leave unchanged.
- Keep the language as spoken.
- For lectures, an extra rule: rewrite English words that were written phonetically in Indic script into Latin spelling, using generic
  examples ("கம்ப்யூட்டர்" → computer) and the "மீன்" → mean example from the brief. Tamil suffixes stay in Tamil script, and this is
  transliteration, not translation.
- Context:
  - For lectures, a one-line subject per recording (e.g. "statistics: mean, median, mode"). In production this would come from the
    class record; here we wrote it after hearing the lecture, which is mildly optimistic.
  - For FLEURS, a neutral context ("general read speech") and an instruction to keep standard native script.
- Output is JSON with the **same segment ids**, corrected in place, so segment timestamps are kept. Requests are sent per lecture window
  (all its segments) and per 5 FLEURS utterances.
- A first prompt version without the explicit "ENGLISH WORDS" rule was too conservative: gpt-4.1-mini changed 1 of 24 lecture segments.
  It is kept as `results/promptv1_*`.

**Guards** (`scripts/llm_guard.py`). A corrected segment is rejected, and the original kept, if any of these hold:
- (1) its edit distance is over 35% of the segment;
- (2) its length ratio is outside 0.7–1.4;
- (3) it romanises native words, i.e. introduces Latin letters with diacritics.

Notes on the guards:
- Distance and length are measured on a **script-agnostic phonetic skeleton**. A raw character distance would reject exactly the wanted
  fix: "ப்ரோக்ராமிங்" → "programming" is about a 100% raw edit but about 0% phonetic.
- Guard (3) was added after we saw Qwen3-8B romanise a whole Tamil segment ("pannuThu paNṟēṅk illāyā…"), which the phonetic guard alone
  had accepted. All runs were then re-guarded offline with `scripts/reguard.py`.
- The raw-character guard would have fired 4–9 times per lecture run (counts in `results/meta/llmfix_*.json`).

**Reading it**

- **FLEURS:**
  - gpt-4.1-mini edits 220 of 225 utterances, mostly spelling and word boundaries. Macro WER goes 16.5 → 15.9, with the biggest gain in
    Malayalam (17.9 → 15.0) and small losses in kn/gu CER.
  - Qwen3-8B edits only 33 of 225, and the WER is unchanged.
  - Neither corrector adds hallucinated words: insertions stay at about 1.5% of reference words, and no FLEURS segment tripped a guard.
  - **The 2-point gap to Saaras remains.**
- **Lectures with IndicConformer:**
  - The LLM restores some English terms (average, mean/mode/median, language, application, password, HTML, CSS). Retention goes 0 →
    14% with GPT and 4% with Qwen.
  - But it cannot bring back the ~70% of speech the recogniser dropped (lec4 stays "நடு நம்பர் மீடிய"), and it sometimes "repairs"
    nonsense into fluent nonsense ("திரோராங்கேஜ் இஸ் ஷோங் யூ" → "storage is show யூ").
  - Agreement CER only goes 84.5 → 77.2.
- **Lectures with Whisper:**
  - There are small, consistent gains: agreement WER 55.0 → 52.9, retention 63 → 67%, and "medium" → "median" fixed in lec4.
  - Inserted words versus Saaras barely move (20 → 23).
  - Whisper's hallucinated fragments are not fixed ("dedansல் எதுcles martial number").
- **Runtime per lecture-hour:**
  - gpt-4.1-mini: 1.7–2.9 min of API latency, sequential, one request per 60 s window. In production the requests would run in parallel.
  - Qwen3-8B: 5.3–11.4 min on the RTX 5050, at ~57 tokens/s generation and ~1,700 tokens/s prompt. VRAM was ~5.6 GB (nvidia-smi:
    5.99 GB total with the desktop, against 0.33 GB idle), and llama-server RAM ~1.3 GB.
  - Tamil costs a lot of tokens: Qwen used 1.5–2.5× more tokens than GPT for the same text.

**Excerpts (original IndicConformer / corrected / Saaras):**

- **lec1 @ 80 s**
  - IC: …போட்டி வச்சு **ஆவரேஜ்** வச்சு எடுக்கும் சரியா எஸ் மோடுன்றது மோஸ்ட் ரிப்பீட்டிங் வேல்யூ…
  - +GPT: …போட்டி வச்சு **average** வச்சு எடுக்கும் சரியா எஸ் மோடுன்றது மோஸ்ட் ரிப்பீட்டிங் வேல்யூ… *(one term fixed, "most repeating value" left in Tamil script)*
  - +Qwen: unchanged
  - Saaras: …போட்டி வச்சு average வச்சு எடுக்கணும். சரியா? Yes, mode-ன்றது most repeating value, most frequent…
- **lec2 @ 600 s**
  - IC: ப்ரோக்ராமிங் லாங்குவேஜ் அப்ளிகேஷன் ரன் பண்ணுது … நேம் பாஸ்வேர்டு கரெக்டா யூ சி வாட் ஸ் திரோராங்கேஜ் இஸ் ஷோங் யூ … எச் டி எம் எல் சி எஸ் எஸ்…
  - +GPT: ப்ரோக்ராமிங் **language application run** பண்ணுது … நேம் **password** கரெக்டா யூ சி வாட் **storage is show** யூ diagramming it is **HTML CSS**…
  - +Qwen: *(romanised the whole segment; rejected by guard 3, original kept)*
  - Saaras: அப்ப programming language தான் application-அ run பண்ணுது. So consider your ERP. ERP-ல login பண்றீங்க இல்லையா?…
- **lec4 @ 200 s**
  - IC: நடு நம்பர் மீடிய
  - +GPT / +Qwen: unchanged (nothing to correct; the speech was never recognised)
  - Whisper+GPT: அதனால் mean தான் **median** எண்ணான் அப்படியே போட்டடுக்கூடாது…
  - Saaras: அதனால மீன் தான் median-னு அப்படியே போட்டுறக்கூடாது…

**Conclusion.** No. **IndicConformer + LLM correction does not match Saaras for our classroom use.** The limit is the recogniser's
recall on noisy, code-mixed classroom audio, not spelling, and a text-only LLM cannot recover audio it never saw. The correction step
itself is cheap and safe with guards:
- **API (gpt-4.1-mini):** ≈ $0.025–0.05 (≈ ₹2–5) per lecture-hour (IndicConformer source: $0.0033 for 8 lecture-minutes; Whisper
  source: $0.007).
- **Local Qwen3-8B Q4:** 5–11 GPU-minutes per lecture-hour on this laptop GPU. On a future L4-class box that is ≈ ₹5–17 per lecture-hour
  if rented by the hour at the assumed ₹60–90/h, or ~₹0 marginal on an owned box that is otherwise idle.

So "STT + LLM" adds ₹2–17 to whatever the STT costs. It is worth keeping as a **light post-processor** (restoring English terms, fixing
spelling) on top of a recogniser that already hears classroom speech well, such as a fine-tuned Whisper or IndicConformer. It is not a
substitute for that fine-tune. If the ASR is fine-tuned to emit Latin English directly, the LLM step becomes optional.

| Provider | Audio sent | Requests | Approx. cost |

| Sarvam saaras:v3 | 61.45 min (3,686.8 s) | 298 (incl. 20 lecture pieces and 3 SSL failures that were retried) | ≈ ₹31 at ₹30/h |
| OpenAI whisper-1 | 61.45 min (3,686.8 s) | 411 (126 were rejected with HTTP 400 `unsupported_language`, 0 s billed per the API response, then re-sent with auto-detect) | ≈ $0.37 |
| OpenAI gpt-4.1-mini (LLM phase) | 34,983 prompt + 17,915 completion tokens (incl. prompt-v1 trial) | 69 | ≈ $0.043 (≈ ₹4) (cap ₹100) at $0.40 / $1.60 per M tokens |

Raw data: `results/<model>.jsonl` has one line per utterance × model (id, set, lang, reference, hypothesis, duration, seconds, plus
segments/detected language where available). Summaries are in `results/summary.csv` and `results/lecture_summary.csv`, the tables in
`results/tables.md`, and per-model load/VRAM/RAM in `results/meta/*.json`.
